newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finmin sees 200 bps fall in rates in '97.
newsitem.headline: Thai finmin sees 200 bps fall in rates in '97.

text.p: Thai finance minister Amnuay Viravan said on Monday financial institutions in the country would probably cut interest rates by 200 basis points in 1997.
"If the interest rates come down it would be easier for businesses to recover," Amnuay said. "The Bank of Thailand must take a lead in cutting the interest rates."
Viravan did not elaborate, but told reporters he had discussed the issue with financial institutions. Thai rates are among the highest in the region and range between 13-13.25 percent.

The central bank has long adopted a policy of keeping domestic interest rates high to attract foreign capital and discourage speculation against the baht, which has been hit hard by the country's financial crisis.
Analysts said the Bank of Thailand's successful efforts last week to halt speculation in the baht may encourage looser monetary policy in the future.

The bank intervened with several other regional central banks in the foreign exchange markets to defend the baht. It also ordered local banks not to sell baht to offshore investors to halt speculation against the currency.
Amnuay also said Thailand plans to balance its budget for the 1997/98 (October/September) fiscal year.

Amnuay, who on Friday said the government planned to trim 26 billion baht ($1 billion) from the 1997/98 budget, said the cuts would not be from investment spending. But they would help the government balance the budget.
Earlier on Monday central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said the government did not plan any more cuts from the current budget, and said he expected a slight budget deficit this year.
Thailand has had a balanced budget for the past nine years.

Rerngchai said Thailand would raise some taxes to offset falling tax revenue. He told reporters after meeting top economic planners that the government would likely raise at least three to four types of taxes this year and in 1998 to raise funds to make up its revenue shortfalls.
